[10] In accordance with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA), I can only admit evidence:
i) that arose after the RPD rendered its decision;
ii) that was not reasonably available at the time of the decision;
iii) that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented to the RPD before the decision was rendered.
iv) If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide whether the evidence is new, credible and relevant before admitting it.2
Letters of testimony

[11] The letters of testimony are not admitted for the reasons set out below. The transcript of the hearing reads as follows:
[Translation]
MEMBER: Was there a document or documents that you wanted to obtain and present to the panel, but that you were unable to obtain?
CLAIMANT: For example?
MEMBER: For example, sometimes, supporting documents are presented, for example, you presented a letter from your spouse, et cetera. So, my question was, are there other documents that you wanted to present, but that you were unable to obtain?
CLAIMANT: No.3

[12] According to the transcript, the appellant was specifically asked if there was any evidence that he was unable to obtain, and he replied no. He could have stated that he wanted to present letters of testimony from his brother and sister, but that he could not do so because they did not have their identity documents, which he did not do. The appellant could have submitted these letters before the hearing and explained at the hearing what he is arguing on appeal. In addition, the letters are not required to be accompanied by identity documents. The appellant does not satisfactorily explain why he waited until October 2024, the date he filed his appeal memorandum, to submit this evidence, when he could have, for example, asked the RPD to grant him a deadline extension after the hearing to submit them, or submitted them before the RPD rendered its decision, which he did not do.

[13] It is worth mentioning that the RPD noted in its decision concerns regarding the lack of letters of testimony from the appellant's family members, notably his brother and sisters, and it seems that by presenting this evidence on appeal, he is trying to complete a deficient record presented to the RPD.
Newspaper articles

[14] I note that the newspaper articles were all published in October 2024, that is, after the RPD's decision. I have no reason to doubt their credibility, and I am of the opinion that they are new and relevant to the analysis of the risk that the appellant would be subjected to if he returned to Haiti. This evidence is admitted.

subthemes.text:
ANALYSIS

[16] I independently assessed all the evidence, listened to the audio recording of the hearing while reading the transcript, and applied the correctness standard.
The Refugee Protection Division erred in its risk assessment

[17] At the hearing, the appellant stated that the fact that he is a government official of a certain rank exposed him to being targeted, due to the assumption that he had money. He also stated that gangs in Haiti can easily distinguish vehicles belonging to government officials through their licence plates.4

[18] The RPD acknowledged that the appellant was a government official in Haiti and that gangs would have identified him through the government vehicle made available to him. It added the following:

[7] ...It was not alleged in testimony or submissions, and there isn't evidence in this respect, that the claimant was targeted for reason of being a government employee as such, beyond the financial motivation of the bandits and their use of his employment as a marker of sufficient financial means to pay ransom.5

[8] I have considered the letter6 from the claimant's ex-spouse, the mother of his child, who is a permanent resident of Canada and had left Haiti some years before the events described above occurred. The letter seeks to explain why the claimant came to Canada, rather than ask for asylum in the United Stated through which country he passed, and states that the claimant was targeted by criminal gangs in Haiti due to his status as a government employee. The author says that her ex-husband was personally targeted because of being automatically associated with the government. While this letter seems to suggest that the claimant was targeted because of his status as a government official, since armed gangs have sought to undermine the state apparatus, I find that the author of the letter has no direct knowledge of the circumstances and while she may hold this opinion, given that the claimant in his sworn testimony clearly identified money as the sole motivation of the bandits, I find that the letter has little probative value when it comes to the nature of the risk for the claimant in Haiti.
[emphasis added]

[19] On appeal, the appellant states the following: [translation] "I am asking the RAD to consider that the appellant would be personally subjected to a very high risk of persecution because of his status as the person responsible for logistics at the ministry of commerce in Haiti."

[20] Respectfully, I am of the opinion that the RPD ignored the allegations in the BOC Form which read as follows:
[Translation]
GIVEN THAT I HAD WORKED AT THE MINISTRY OF XXXX FOR SEVERAL YEARS, I WAS AUTOMATICALLY ASSOCIATED WITH MEMBERS OF THE GOVERNMENT WHO, ACCORDING TO CITIZENS AND GANGS, ARE RESPONSIBLE FOR HAITIANS' MISERY.6
[emphasis added]

[21] Although the appellant stated many times at the hearing that the gangs found his profile appealing (financial motivation), the fact remains that, in his BOC Form, he clearly mentions the population's and gangs' discontent as a sign of opposition to the Haitian government's functioning. The appellant alleges that he was associated with the government and held responsible for the population's misery. The RPD therefore erred by failing to analyze the appellant's allegations in this regard. It erred by stating in its decision "that there isn't evidence in this respect, that the claimant was targeted for reason of being a government employee as such," whereas the written account clearly mentions this. The RPD should have questioned the appellant further about the allegations in his BOC Form, and not only about what he stated at the hearing. This error is determinative because it concerns the incorrect risk assessment that the RPD's decision was based on.
Letter of testimony from the appellant's ex-spouse

[22] In support of his refugee protection claim, the appellant submitted a letter of testimony from his ex-spouse in which she states that he was targeted in Haiti because of his duties at the ministry of XXXX XXXX XXXX.7

[23] The RPD did not assign any probative value to this letter because it was of the opinion that the ex-spouse did not witness the events and that the appellant clearly stated in his testimony that money was the sole motivation of the bandits.

[24] At the risk of repeating myself, the RPD should have assessed this letter based on all the evidence, especially the allegations in the BOC Form that the refugee protection claim was based on, and not the testimony alone. The RPD erred by being selective with the evidence.
Kidnapping involving the appellant's brother

[25] The RPD found the appellant's allegations that his brother was kidnapped by gangs and released in exchange for a ransom to be credible. At the hearing, he stated that he believed that he had been the intended victim of the kidnapping, but since he was not at home, the criminals instead kidnapped his brother, who was visiting him at that time.

[26] The RPD was of the opinion that the evidence was insufficient to conclude that there was any link between the two instances of the appellant being followed near his workplace by unidentified persons, and unidentified persons kidnapping his brother for ransom. It was of the opinion that the fact that the kidnappers called him to request a ransom demonstrates that they were able to identify him as the resident of the place where the kidnapping occurred and find out his contact information, namely, his telephone number. It states the following:
It is not known whether the kidnappers were the same persons who had followed the claimant or belonged to the same gang. Even if this were the case, identifying the claimant as a potential target for kidnapping because of the perception that, as a government employee, he was wealthy, does not constitute personal risk in the meaning of s. 97(1)b of the IRPA, since it is not personal to him - it applies to a portion of the population.
[emphasis added]

[27] On appeal, the appellant states the following:
[Translation]
This conclusion is incorrect because the panel considered a fact or an aspect of the appellant's testimony in an isolated manner rather than taking into account the appellant's general situation and considering overall his personal situation and the risks that he would be personally subjected to.... Moreover, the appellant did not base his refugee protection claim on any generalized risk in Haiti or on the perception of wealth. The RPD took the appellant's statements out of context.... This conclusion could be the result of an incorrect assessment of the prospective risks in accordance with the criteria established by the Federal Court.

[28] I agree with the appellant. It is worth mentioning that the RPD set the bar high in its analysis of the lack of a link between the events alleged in the BOC Form. It used the words "is not known," whereas the standard of proof is the balance of probabilities. The appellant alleges that he was followed by criminals twice. He claims that they identified him through the licence plate of the vehicle he was driving. He claims that his brother was kidnapped. These events allegedly took place between XXXX and XXXX 2022. At the risk of repeating myself, the RPD only assessed the gangs' financial motivation, "perception of wealth," whereas the appellant alleges in his BOC Form that gangs targeted him because of his duties at the ministry of commerce and industry. The RPD should have assessed these important aspects, which it did not do.

[21] Although the appellant stated many times at the hearing that the gangs found his profile appealing (financial motivation), the fact remains that, in his BOC Form, he clearly mentions the population's and gangs' discontent as a sign of opposition to the Haitian government's functioning. The appellant alleges that he was associated with the government and held responsible for the population's misery. The RPD therefore erred by failing to analyze the appellant's allegations in this regard. It erred by stating in its decision "that there isn't evidence in this respect, that the claimant was targeted for reason of being a government employee as such," whereas the written account clearly mentions this. The RPD should have questioned the appellant further about the allegations in his BOC Form, and not only about what he stated at the hearing. This error is determinative because it concerns the incorrect risk assessment that the RPD's decision was based on.
Letter of testimony from the appellant's ex-spouse

[22] In support of his refugee protection claim, the appellant submitted a letter of testimony from his ex-spouse in which she states that he was targeted in Haiti because of his duties at the ministry of XXXX XXXX XXXX.7

[23] The RPD did not assign any probative value to this letter because it was of the opinion that the ex-spouse did not witness the events and that the appellant clearly stated in his testimony that money was the sole motivation of the bandits.

[24] At the risk of repeating myself, the RPD should have assessed this letter based on all the evidence, especially the allegations in the BOC Form that the refugee protection claim was based on, and not the testimony alone. The RPD erred by being selective with the evidence.

[25] The RPD found the appellant's allegations that his brother was kidnapped by gangs and released in exchange for a ransom to be credible. At the hearing, he stated that he believed that he had been the intended victim of the kidnapping, but since he was not at home, the criminals instead kidnapped his brother, who was visiting him at that time.

[26] The RPD was of the opinion that the evidence was insufficient to conclude that there was any link between the two instances of the appellant being followed near his workplace by unidentified persons, and unidentified persons kidnapping his brother for ransom. It was of the opinion that the fact that the kidnappers called him to request a ransom demonstrates that they were able to identify him as the resident of the place where the kidnapping occurred and find out his contact information, namely, his telephone number. It states the following:
It is not known whether the kidnappers were the same persons who had followed the claimant or belonged to the same gang. Even if this were the case, identifying the claimant as a potential target for kidnapping because of the perception that, as a government employee, he was wealthy, does not constitute personal risk in the meaning of s. 97(1)b of the IRPA, since it is not personal to him - it applies to a portion of the population.
[emphasis added]

[27] On appeal, the appellant states the following:
[Translation]
This conclusion is incorrect because the panel considered a fact or an aspect of the appellant's testimony in an isolated manner rather than taking into account the appellant's general situation and considering overall his personal situation and the risks that he would be personally subjected to.... [28] I agree with the appellant. It is worth mentioning that the RPD set the bar high in its analysis of the lack of a link between the events alleged in the BOC Form. The RPD should have assessed these important aspects, which it did not do.

[29] My analysis ends there because the RPD's errors essentially concern the determinative issue, both for the RPD and the RAD, namely, the nature of the risk that the appellant would be subjected to if he returned to Haiti.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] I allow the appeal and refer the matter for re-determination by a differently constituted panel of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD). XXXX XXXX (the appellant) is a citizen of Haiti. His refugee protection claim was heard before the RPD on July 17, 2024, and rejected on August 13, 2024. He is appealing this decision.

[2] In his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the appellant alleges that gangs targeted him because of his duties at the ministry of XXXX XXXX XXXX. He alleges that his brother was kidnapped and released in exchange for a ransom.
[3] The RPD found the appellant's allegations credible, but it rejected his claim on the grounds that he would be subjected to a generalized risk of criminal activity.
[4] On appeal, the appellant submitted new evidence and states that the RPD erred in its analysis of the nature of the risk that he would be subjected to in Haiti.
[5] The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD erred in its assessment of the nature of the risk.

[6] My answer to the determinative issue is yes, and I am of the opinion that the RPD ignored an important element from the written account accompanying the BOC Form in its analysis.
NEW EVIDENCE

[7] On appeal, the appellant submitted the following evidence:
- Letter of testimony from his sister, dated October 22, 2024, accompanied by a photograph of an identity document.
- Letter of testimony from his brother, dated October 22, 2024, accompanied by a photograph of an identity document.
- Four newspaper articles regarding the violence and insecurity in Haiti.

[8] In their testimony, the brother and sister state that they fled Haiti for the Dominican Republic out of fear that the gangs would target them. They state that the appellant was targeted because of his duties at the ministry of XXXX XXXX XXXX. The appellant's brother adds that he was kidnapped and released in exchange for a ransom paid by his brother (the appellant).

[9] The appellant states that he was unable to obtain this evidence before the hearing because his brother and sister fled Haiti for the Dominican Republic, leaving behind all their personal belongings, notably their identity documents.
Not all the evidence submitted by the appellant is admitted

[11] The letters of testimony are not admitted for the reasons set out below. The transcript of the hearing reads as follows:
[Translation]
MEMBER: Was there a document or documents that you wanted to obtain and present to the panel, but that you were unable to obtain?
CLAIMANT: For example?
MEMBER: For example, sometimes, supporting documents are presented, for example, you presented a letter from your spouse, et cetera. So, my question was, are there other documents that you wanted to present, but that you were unable to obtain?
CLAIMANT: No.3

[12] According to the transcript, the appellant was specifically asked if there was any evidence that he was unable to obtain, and he replied no. He could have stated that he wanted to present letters of testimony from his brother and sister, but that he could not do so because they did not have their identity documents, which he did not do. The appellant could have submitted these letters before the hearing and explained at the hearing what he is arguing on appeal. In addition, the letters are not required to be accompanied by identity documents. The appellant does not satisfactorily explain why he waited until October 2024, the date he filed his appeal memorandum, to submit this evidence, when he could have, for example, asked the RPD to grant him a deadline extension after the hearing to submit them, or submitted them before the RPD rendered its decision, which he did not do.

[13] It is worth mentioning that the RPD noted in its decision concerns regarding the lack of letters of testimony from the appellant's family members, notably his brother and sisters, and it seems that by presenting this evidence on appeal, he is trying to complete a deficient record presented to the RPD.
Newspaper articles

[14] I note that the newspaper articles were all published in October 2024, that is, after the RPD's decision. I have no reason to doubt their credibility, and I am of the opinion that they are new and relevant to the analysis of the risk that the appellant would be subjected to if he returned to Haiti. This evidence is admitted.
Request for an oral hearing

[15] On appeal, the appellant submitted a request for an oral hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA. Although some evidence was admitted under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, the fact remains that it does not raise a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the appellant. The criteria in subsection 110(6) of the IRPA are not met, and the RAD must proceed without holding an oral hearing.
ANALYSIS

[16] I independently assessed all the evidence, listened to the audio recording of the hearing while reading the transcript, and applied the correctness standard.
The Refugee Protection Division erred in its risk assessment

[17] At the hearing, the appellant stated that the fact that he is a government official of a certain rank exposed him to being targeted, due to the assumption that he had money. He also stated that gangs in Haiti can easily distinguish vehicles belonging to government officials through their licence plates.4
[18] The RPD acknowledged that the appellant was a government official in Haiti and that gangs would have identified him through the government vehicle made available to him. It added the following:

[7] ...It was not alleged in testimony or submissions, and there isn't evidence in this respect, that the claimant was targeted for reason of being a government employee as such, beyond the financial motivation of the bandits and their use of his employment as a marker of sufficient financial means to pay ransom.5

[8] I have considered the letter6 from the claimant's ex-spouse, the mother of his child, who is a permanent resident of Canada and had left Haiti some years before the events described above occurred. The letter seeks to explain why the claimant came to Canada, rather than ask for asylum in the United Stated through which country he passed, and states that the claimant was targeted by criminal gangs in Haiti due to his status as a government employee. The author says that her ex-husband was personally targeted because of being automatically associated with the government. While this letter seems to suggest that the claimant was targeted because of his status as a government official, since armed gangs have sought to undermine the state apparatus, I find that the author of the letter has no direct knowledge of the circumstances and while she may hold this opinion, given that the claimant in his sworn testimony clearly identified money as the sole motivation of the bandits, I find that the letter has little probative value when it comes to the nature of the risk for the claimant in Haiti.
[emphasis added]

[19] On appeal, the appellant states the following: [translation] "I am asking the RAD to consider that the appellant would be personally subjected to a very high risk of persecution because of his status as the person responsible for logistics at the ministry of commerce in Haiti."

It states the following:
It is not known whether the kidnappers were the same persons who had followed the claimant or belonged to the same gang. Even if this were the case, identifying the claimant as a potential target for kidnapping because of the perception that, as a government employee, he was wealthy, does not constitute personal risk in the meaning of s. 97(1)b of the IRPA, since it is not personal to him - it applies to a portion of the population.
[emphasis added]

[Translation]
This conclusion is incorrect because the panel considered a fact or an aspect of the appellant's testimony in an isolated manner rather than taking into account the appellant's general situation and considering overall his personal situation and the risks that he would be personally subjected to.... Moreover, the appellant did not base his refugee protection claim on any generalized risk in Haiti or on the perception of wealth. The RPD took the appellant's statements out of context.... [29] My analysis ends there because the RPD's errors essentially concern the determinative issue, both for the RPD and the RAD, namely, the nature of the risk that the appellant would be subjected to if he returned to Haiti.
CONCLUSION

[30] I allow the appeal and refer the matter for re-determination before a differently constituted RPD panel.
